title: Thrissur biker killed by dangerous load of iron rods, MVD to suspend driver's licence
content: The death of 47-year-old Sherin P John, a native of Ollur, after iron rods fell on him from a moving pickup van has once again raised serious concerns over road safety and the unsafe transportation of goods. The accident took place on August 21 near HiLITE Mall on the Thrissur-Kuttanellur road. Sherin was riding his motorcycle when a pickup van driven by Suresh, which was trailing him, braked abruptly to avoid an autorickshaw. The long iron rods tied to the top of the vehicle slipped and fell on Sherin, killing him. The Motor Vehicles Department has decided to suspend the licence of the vehicle's driver. CCTV visuals of the incident have also raised questions about speeding, reckless driving and improper traffic conduct on the road. Joint RTO (Enforcement) Justin Maliakkal told Onmanorama that the vehicle's load was both illegal and improperly secured. "The rods were not properly secured and were liable to slip. When the vehicle applied sudden brakes after the autorickshaw came into view, they slipped and fell on Sherin," he said. He added that the driver's licence would be suspended for at least six months and that he would be required to attend classes at a training centre in Edappal. Under section 194 of the Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019, carrying loads that project beyond the vehicle attracts a mandatory 20,000 fine for registered vehicle owners. However, officials admit that strict enforcement against smaller commercial vehicles is often tricky. Motor Vehicle Inspector Vinod Kumar N said that while owners of heavy goods vehicles can generally afford to pay the fines, small vehicle operators often struggle to do so. "Under the revised rules, carrying loads that project beyond the permissible limit attracts a 20,000 fine for the registered owner. The penalty applies to all vehicles found carrying such loads. However, small pickup vehicles often carry relatively small loads for short-distance transportation. When fines are imposed, the operators often cannot afford to pay them. Officials also face public backlash and when the rules are strictly enforced, some even threaten suicide," he said. Officials said they are often forced to take a lenient approach on humanitarian grounds, imposing minimal fines. They added that meaningful change can happen only when those transporting goods take responsibility for ensuring that their loads are carried safely. "In this case, the court will now impose the 20,000 fine on Suresh," Vinod said. Ollur police arrested Suresh under Sections 281 (rash or negligent driving that endangers human life) and 106(1) (causing a person's death by a rash or negligent act) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). Police said he has been remanded in custody pending further investigation.
